problem: Existing navigation benchmarks score agents on success rate, collision rate, SPL and path length. These metrics say nothing about the cost and revenue that decide whether an autonomous delivery robot can be commercialised.
motivation: Operating cost is the main driver of adopting delivery robots, yet navigation research has no economic yardstick. Behaviours that task metrics ignore, such as sharp turns that spill food, pedestrian contacts and property damage, carry real monetary cost. The paper therefore converts physics-simulated behaviour into CAPEX, OPEX, revenue and break-even analysis, using parameters from SEC filings, AIS injury data and market prices.
key_idea: Evaluate navigation policies by contribution margin and break-even point, mapping Isaac Sim collision and cargo dynamics through real-world-referenced cost and revenue models.
insight: High task success does not imply economic viability: all seven baselines have negative contribution margins, and pedestrian-safety cost is the largest modelled OPEX component. The least-negative margin overall (NavDP) is an artefact of a policy that barely moves, so revenue and OPEX both stay near zero. Among methods with non-zero SLA compliance, CANVAS has the least-negative margin. Its teleoperation training data was collected with an instruction to drive smoothly, and it gets the lowest timeout rate, whereas Nav2's DWB planner keeps forward speed while evading and so spoils more food. The paper reports that setting the pedestrian term to zero still leaves every margin negative.
method: Economic model: profit = revenue − (CAPEX + OPEX × N). Contribution margin = R − OPEX, and BEP = CAPEX / margin, which is undefined when the margin is negative. R = delivery fee × SLA compliance.
CAPEX: hardware (Segway E1 robot price, plus LiDAR and GPS where used) and teleoperation data-collection cost for learning-based methods (wage × collected hours).

OPEX: electricity from simulated power and runtime; repair cost scaled by the ratio of simulated physical-assistance events to the real-world rate; service compensation for spoiled, timeout and physical-assistance failures; pedestrian safety cost; property damage cost.
Pedestrian safety cost: collision Δv is mapped to a probability over AIS injury severities, priced with NHTSA crash costs and scaled by a robot/vehicle mass-ratio factor.
Property damage cost: contacts above 100 N·s with bollards, mailboxes, trash bins and building glass are priced at municipal replacement rates.

Simulation environment: Isaac Sim, 200 m × 200 m urban sidewalk map with pedestrians and priced obstacles, a Segway E1 with popcorn cargo and jerk-based food spoilage, and SLA/timeout/physical-assistance episode outcomes.

Baselines: Nav2 with AMCL or GPS-only localization; GNM, ViNT, NoMaD, NavDP and CANVAS finetuned on a CostNav teleoperation dataset. CANVAS is modified to output velocity commands end-to-end via the FAST tokenizer.
Sim-to-real check: the same CANVAS checkpoint is deployed on a real Segway E1 (Livox LiDAR localization, off-board laptop) over 8 sidewalk scenarios and compared with simulation.

setting.backbone: Benchmark paper. Baselines: Nav2 (DWB planner, AMCL/GPS), GNM, ViNT, NoMaD, NavDP, and CANVAS (VLA-style policy with FAST tokenizer, fine-tuned).
setting.training_data: Learning baselines start from their official pretrained checkpoints (GNM 70 hr real, ViNT 80 hr real, NoMaD 100+ hr real, NavDP 363 km sim, CANVAS 48 hr / 219 km sim) and are finetuned on the CostNav teleoperation dataset. Its hours are a LaTeX macro, so the exact value is not visible. Rule-based Nav2 needs no training.
setting.observation: Varies by baseline: LiDAR + GPS (Nav2); monocular RGB (GNM/ViNT/NoMaD); RGB-D (NavDP); RGB + GPS (CANVAS, plus a top-down sketch goal).
setting.action_space: Continuous velocity commands (CANVAS via FAST tokens); Nav2 uses DWB local planning; other baselines output waypoints/velocities.
setting.simulator: NVIDIA Isaac Sim (PhysX 5); real-world validation on a Segway E1.
setting.privileged: Nav2 uses a prebuilt occupancy map (rule-based mapping cost is not counted); the CANVAS goal is a sketch of the simulator's shortest path; topological image goals come from the environment map.

numbers_note: The paper's results tables (Tables 2, 3 and the sim-to-real table) are filled by LaTeX macros (e.g. \CMarginCANVAS, \SEpisodeTermSLACANVAS) whose values are not in the provided source, so no exact printed values could be copied. Evaluation counts are also macros; the real-world run is 8 scenarios, with 5 of 8 successful per the appendix. The benchmark is also not one of the canonical names, and no SR/SPL are reported.
results: All seven baselines have negative contribution margins, so none reaches break-even. CANVAS (RGB + GPS) has the highest task success and the least-negative margin among methods with non-zero SLA compliance, ahead of LiDAR-equipped Nav2 with GPS. GNM, NoMaD and NavDP have near-zero SLA compliance, and ViNT has frequent physical-assistance events and the worst margin. On the real Segway E1, CANVAS's SLA compliance is close to its simulation value.
limitations: Event counts come from simulation and are only partially validated in the real world (8 scenarios, one route). The pedestrian-injury cost is a proxy rescaled by mass from passenger-vehicle data and is not calibrated against real robot-pedestrian contact rates.
The economic model omits training compute, rule-based mapping cost, demand and dynamic pricing, and failure modes such as battery depletion.
It is a single setup: one robot, popcorn cargo, one urban map, daytime only. Some baselines reach ≤10% SLA and may not have been tuned for the setup, so rankings are not each method's ceiling.
